4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The final chapter of Colossians is shorter and more personal than the preceding chapters but carries the letter’s theology into two final areas: the Christian’s relationship to prayer and to the world (vv. 2–6), and the network of relationships through which the gospel advances (vv. 7–18). Together they show the gospel in its two directions: upward (prayer) and outward (mission), and the community of people in whom those directions are embodied.

The instructions on prayer and conduct (vv. 2–6) are brief but theologically dense. Prayer requires steadfastness and watchfulness — active, alert engagement rather than routine. Thanksgiving is its constant accompaniment. The prayer for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — the mystery Paul himself is imprisoned for proclaiming — is the prayer of a man for whom the gospel’s advance is more important than his own comfort or release. Conduct toward outsiders is to be “in wisdom,” making the best use of the time, with speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” — the attractive, preserving, flavour-giving quality that makes the gospel winsome as well as true.

The closing personal greetings reveal the extraordinary network of relationships through which the gospel was advancing in the first century: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark (the John Mark of Acts 15, apparently reconciled with Paul), Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nympha and her house church, Archippus. These are not decorative biographical details; they are the human face of the gospel’s advance, the community of grace in its concrete, particular, named reality.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Masters” translates kyrioi — the very same word as “Lord.” In the Roman world a master held near-absolute power over his slaves: he could command, punish, sell, and in law even kill them, with little accountability. A slave was reckoned property — Aristotle had called him “a living tool” — an economic asset valued for what he produced, not a person with rights, and the duties of the household ran one way only, from slave up to master. That is what makes this verse quietly revolutionary: Paul turns and addresses the masters, and lays an obligation on them. The bridge to our world is the employer — the boss, the manager, the business owner, anyone who holds power over other people’s work and livelihood. The old temptation survives intact: to see workers as “resources” (we even say human resources), replaceable cogs valued only for output and the bottom line.

“Treat your bondservants justly and fairly.” “Justly” means to render what is right and due — honest dealing, fair provision, discipline that is just and not arbitrary. “Fairly” is literally equity — even-handed, impartial treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is your equal and your brother. This went far beyond anything Roman law asked: the one-way street becomes two-way, and the slave is suddenly a person to whom justice is owed — think of Philemon, told to welcome a runaway back as a “beloved brother” (Philem. 16).

And it lands squarely in the corporate world: a fair wage, honest contracts kept, safe conditions, no favouritism, no exploitation, no treating human beings as disposable. It looks like the owner who shares the gain fairly, the manager who disciplines by principle rather than mood, the boss who treats the night cleaner and the senior partner with the same human dignity. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town.

And here is the whole motive, a master-stroke of wording: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man who holds the power is himself a servant; over the one at the top of the earthly ladder stands One who owns him utterly. So Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up: deal justly with those beneath you, because you will answer for it to the Lord above you — the same Lord who “shows no partiality” (3:25).

The master’s wealth and rank buy him nothing at that throne. And there is a humbling sweetness folded in: master and slave have the same Master in heaven — they kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made and bought them both. At the foot of the cross the boss and the worker are two sinners saved by the same grace, and the Christian who holds authority wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow-servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder (cf. Eph. 6:9; Lev. 25:43).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s closing instructions begin where the new life always begins — on its knees. “Continue steadfastly in prayer,” he says, and the very command is a comfort, for he would not have to urge perseverance if prayer were easy to sustain. Three notes mark the praying he calls for: it is to be steadfast (dogged and persevering, not occasional), watchful (awake and alert, the sentry who will not doze, never a drowsy mumble), and thankful (saturated with gratitude, which guards prayer from collapsing into a mere list of wants and fuels the very perseverance he has just commanded). A church that prays like this will not easily be carried off by any false teacher.

Then comes the request that startles — for it comes from a man in chains. Paul asks not for the prison door to open but for “a door for the word”: his concern is not his own freedom but the gospel’s. And he, the great apostle, asks a church he has never met to pray for him — proof that none of us, however gifted, outgrows the need of God’s help and his people’s prayers. He longs to declare “the mystery of Christ” — the long-hidden, now-revealed secret who is a Person — and even prays for the plain clarity of his own preaching, presuming nothing on his eloquence. And he names the cause of his imprisonment without a breath of complaint against Rome or against God: he is simply the prisoner of Christ Jesus, resting in the sovereign hand that set him there for the gospel’s advance.

From the church’s prayer Paul turns to its public face before the watching world. Believers are to “walk in wisdom toward outsiders” — living with such integrity and winsomeness that their conduct adorns the gospel rather than repelling people from it, avoiding both compromise with the world and a sour, superior aloofness from it. They are to be “making the best use of the time” — buying up every fleeting opportunity, as a shrewd merchant snaps up a bargain, to do good and to point to Christ before the moment passes. And their speech is to be “gracious, seasoned with salt” — kind and flavourful, winsome and wholesome, neither bland nor cutting — so that they are ready to give a fitting, tailored answer to each person who asks about the hope that is in them. Wise conduct and gracious speech are how a church wins a hearing for the gospel it prays God to advance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Continue steadfastly in prayer” — the word means to persevere, to hold fast, to stick doggedly at a thing (the same word used of the first church, who “devoted themselves” to prayer, Acts 2:42). And the very fact that Paul must command it tells us something tender: staying steadfast in prayer is hard, and we need the encouragement. Why so hard?

Because prayer is hidden, unseen labour with no visible machinery; because answers often tarry and we grow discouraged; because the flesh is weak and prayer can feel like “doing nothing”; and because there is an enemy who would far rather we did anything than pray. So Paul does not say “pray when you feel like it” but “keep at it” — it was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Do not measure your praying by how it feels; simply do not stop.

“Being watchful in it” means to stay awake, alert, on guard — the sentry on night watch who dare not doze; it carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said, “Watch and pray” (Matt. 26:41). To be watchful is to pray awake (mind genuinely present, not a drowsy mumble with a wandering heart), with open eyes (alert to what actually needs praying for, and expectant for God’s answer like a watchman looking for the dawn), and vigilant — for prayer’s great enemy is not so much hostility as drowsiness, the half-asleep going-through-the-motions that empties prayer of life.

And “with thanksgiving” sounds, for the fifth time in this short letter (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17), now woven right into prayer. It keeps prayer from collapsing into a mere list of demands, lifting the eyes from what we lack to all God has already given — and that backward look fuels the perseverance Paul just commanded, for the grateful pray-er is the persevering pray-er. We come not to wring favours from a reluctant stranger but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son (cf. Phil. 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Pray also for us” — stop and feel the weight of this. Paul, the apostle chosen by the risen Christ, caught up to the third heaven, a writer of Scripture, planter of churches across the empire, turns to a small congregation he has never even met and asks them to pray for him. The greatest Christian of the age leaning on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers. The lesson is humbling: even the best and most mature of us never outgrows his need of God’s help and his brothers’ prayers — and it cuts the other way too. The humblest saint’s prayers truly count; your prayers for your pastor are no formality, but move the hand that moves the world (cf. Rom. 15:30; Eph. 6:19).

What does he ask them to pray? “That God may open to us a door for the word.” The “open door” is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Cor. 16:9) — and mark two things. First, it is God who opens it; even the chance to share Christ is a gift of his providence, not the fruit of our cleverness. Second, and tenderly: a man in chains does not ask for the prison door to open — he asks for a door for the word.

His own freedom is not his concern; the gospel’s is. “I am bound with chains, but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). And it is “the mystery of Christ” he longs to declare — the same good news, but the richer word: a mystery is a secret long hidden in the heart of God and now thrown open (1:26–27), and it presses the point that the gospel is not a system or a secret technique (as the false teachers offered their initiates) but a Person — “God’s mystery, which is Christ” (2:2).

Then, quietly, one of the wonders of this letter: “on account of which I am in prison” — and not a word of complaint. Paul names the reason for his chains without a trace of grumbling: not against Rome, not against his accusers, not against God, and not a breath of self-pity. He does not see himself as a victim of injustice or bad luck; he looks past the magistrates and soldiers to the sovereign hand behind them and calls himself not the prisoner of Caesar but “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Eph. 3:1). He so believed in the reign of God that he could write, from a cell, “what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Phil. 1:12). That is what it looks like to truly believe God is sovereign — peace where there might have been bitterness, purpose where there might have been despair.

And it searches us: what do we do with our own “prisons” — the unjust treatment, the shut door, the hard providence? Grumble at people and at God, or trust the sovereign hand and ask how Christ might be made known even here? Finally he asks prayer not only for an open door but for a clear word — “that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.” Even the most gifted preacher the church has known does not presume on his own eloquence but asks for prayer to speak plainly; an open door is wasted without a clear message on the far side of it. Pray it for your preachers; pray it for yourself, whenever you try to explain the hope that is in you (cf. Eph. 6:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has asked them to pray for his witness (vv.3–4); now he turns to theirs — how the church commends Christ to “outsiders.” The two belong together: pray for the gospel’s advance, and live so as to advance it. This is no abrupt change of subject but the natural outward movement of the whole letter — having set forth the supremacy of Christ, the new life, the transformed home, and devoted prayer, Paul now sends that new life out to the watching world; the Christ who has filled them is meant to overflow toward those who do not yet know him. “Outsiders” are the non-Christians among whom they live, and Paul cares greatly how the church appears to them, for the world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it.

“Walk in wisdom toward outsiders” — “walk” is the whole conduct of life, and “in wisdom” means with the skill, discernment, and tact of the wisdom hidden in Christ (2:3), knowing how to live before non-Christians in a way that adorns the gospel rather than repelling people from it. So it looks like integrity — honest in business, reliable in your word; like genuine kindness and being a good neighbour; like a blameless life that disarms criticism (1 Pet. 2:12); like the tact to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. It avoids two ditches at once: compromise (blending into the world) and harsh superiority (the sour, judgmental believer the world rightly recoils from).

The only offence we should ever give is the offence of the gospel itself — never the offence of our rudeness, hypocrisy, or foolishness. In pagan Colossae it meant the Christian who was honest in the market and would not join the drunken temple feasts, yet was no sneering prig; today it is the believer at work who is diligent and will not gossip or cut corners, the neighbour quick to help, the Christian online who does not meet every quarrel with cruelty. Your daily conduct before your unbelieving workmates is itself either an argument for Christ or against him.

“Making the best use of the time” — the phrase is vivid: literally “buying up the opportunity,” and the word for time is not the ticking clock (chronos) but the opportune moment (kairos), the open window; the picture is a shrewd merchant snapping up a bargain before it is gone. It means seizing every God-given opening to commend Christ before it passes — “because the days are evil,” as the parallel adds (Eph. 5:16). Opportunities are fleeting and life is short, so make the most of every encounter: the colleague going through a hard season, the unexpected question about your hope, the moment to help or speak a word for Christ. That open window with this neighbour or that relative may not come again; buy it up.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt.” Note the sweep — always, all your talk, not merely your “religious” talk — and the two qualities that mark it. “Gracious” (literally “with grace”) means speech that is kind and winsome, and more, speech that actually gives grace to those who hear it (Eph. 4:29), as the “gracious words” that fell from the lips of Jesus drew the crowds (Luke 4:22). “Seasoned with salt” draws on what salt did — it gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling; so salted speech is not bland, insipid talk but speech with savour, interest, wit, and substance, worth listening to, and wholesome, free of what is corrupt or coarse. (This is the opposite of the modern sense of “salty” speech, which is crude; Paul means tasteful and lively, not foul.)

Hold the two together and you see the balance. Speech that is gracious but not salted is kind but bland — mushy, gushing, saying nothing memorable. Speech that is salted but not gracious is clever but cruel, witty at another’s expense. The Christian’s tongue is to be both at once: kind and interesting, warm and with bite, truthful and winsome — just as the Lord spoke words that drew people in yet carried point and stayed in the memory. In practice it is answering a hostile remark with unexpected kindness rather than defensiveness, speaking a hard truth seasoned so it can be heard rather than blurted to wound, trading the coarse joke and the sour complaint for words that leave a good taste and build people up. Let your talk at the workbench and the kitchen table be neither sour and harsh nor limp and dull, but gracious words with a wholesome tang that make people glad to listen.

And the aim of it all: “so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” — to be ready to give a fitting reply to each one who asks. Mark “each person” — not a single canned formula fired off at everyone, but an answer suited to this individual, his question, his objection, his need. What sort of questions? The watching world’s honest enquiries and challenges about the faith — “why do you live like that?”, “why are you so hopeful?” Peter says the same: “always be prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet with gentleness and respect” (1 Pet. 3:15).

See how the verse hangs together: gracious, flavourful speech is the soil, and readiness to answer is the fruit — a believer whose everyday words are winsome will draw people to ask, and be ready, when they do, to answer that person well; whereas harsh or insipid talk shuts the conversation before it begins. You need not have a sermon by heart; you need a gracious, salted tongue and a heart ready to give this workmate a wise, kind, fitting word about the hope that is in you (cf. Prov. 15:23).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter ends not with a flourish of doctrine but with a page of names — and a modern reader must not skim them, for this closing roll-call is the gospel in its concrete, human form. Here is a living network of real people bound together by Christ, and the words Paul keeps reaching for tell the story: “beloved brother,” “faithful minister,” “fellow servant,” “fellow prisoner,” “a comfort to me.” And look who stands in the circle: Jews and Gentiles in one mission, Luke the educated physician beside Onesimus the runaway slave, Nympha the woman with a whole church in her house. The very walls Paul said Christ had thrown down (3:11) lie flat before our eyes; “Christ is all, and in all” has come all the way down to a list of friends.

Two names make the heart swell. Onesimus, the runaway slave, is sent home not as a criminal but as “our faithful and beloved brother” — the Roman social order quietly overturned in a phrase. And Mark, who once abandoned Paul mid-mission and split him from Barnabas, is here restored and welcomed — grace does not discard those who fail, it remakes them.

(A sober shadow falls too: Demas, named here among the faithful, will one day desert for love of this present world.) At the centre kneels Epaphras, the church’s founder, “always struggling” in prayer — the athlete’s straining word — that they would “stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God,” which is the whole letter distilled into a single petition. These are Paul’s “fellow workers for the kingdom of God” — the kingdom into which, this very letter has said, believers have already been transferred (1:13), and for whose advance they now labour as they await its coming in glory.

Then the apostle takes the pen from his secretary’s hand: “I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.” It is at once a seal of the letter’s genuineness and a touch of pure affection — and then, in his own script, “Remember my chains.” The whole soaring letter on the supremacy of Christ was written by a prisoner, and the chains are themselves an argument, for no one wears irons for a lie. And the last word answers the first: the letter that opened “grace to you” (1:2) closes “grace be with you.” To a church tempted to climb to God by rules and secret knowledge, the final word is the first word — grace, from beginning to end, all the way home.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A modern reader is tempted to skim a page of ancient names. Do not. This closing roll-call is a photograph of the gospel at work, and it quietly preaches everything the letter has argued. Listen to the words Paul keeps reaching for across these verses — “beloved brother,” “faithful minister,” “fellow servant,” “fellow prisoner,” “a comfort to me.” These are not colleagues. They are family, sharing one mission, one suffering, one Lord.

Three of those phrases land on one man, and he is the reason the Colossians are holding this letter at all. Tychicus is the courier. He carried these pages from Paul’s prison to Colossae with Onesimus walking beside him, and he carried the letter we call Ephesians on the same journey (Eph. 6:21–22). A native of the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), he was trusted with Paul’s correspondence more than once.

But notice that Paul does not send him merely to deliver paper. “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts.” Two jobs, and the second is the larger. Tychicus is to tell them how Paul is faring — a church that had never met Paul was anxious about him — and then to encourage their hearts, the same verb Paul used in 2:2 of his own longing for them.

There is a whole doctrine of ministry hidden in that. The word of God arrived at Colossae in the hands of a man whose commission was to love the people he was sent to. It has never travelled any other way. Scripture reaches most people through somebody — a parent, a preacher, a friend who would not give up on them — and the messenger’s character is not incidental to the message. Paul could have sent a courier. He sent a brother.

And observe what Tychicus was not given: any authority over the Colossians, any brief to inspect or correct them. Paul had plenty he could have said to a church flirting with false teaching. The man he sends is sent to reassure. Sometimes the most useful thing you can carry into a troubled congregation is not a correction but your own steady presence.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is one of the great sentences of the New Testament hiding in a list of names. “Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.”

We know exactly who this is, because Paul wrote a whole letter about him. Onesimus was a slave in the household of Philemon, a Colossian Christian. He had run — and in Roman law a runaway slave was a criminal whose owner could have him branded on the forehead, flogged, or crucified, and who could expect no sympathy from any magistrate in the empire. He is now walking back into the town he fled, carrying a letter.

And read how Paul introduces him to the congregation that knew him as somebody’s runaway property. Not “Onesimus, whom I am returning to his master.” Not a word about his legal position. “Our faithful and beloved brother” — the identical phrase he has just used of Tychicus, a free man and an apostolic delegate. The two men are given the same titles in the same breath, and the Colossians are to receive them on the same terms.

Then four words that go further still: “who is one of you.” He is not an outsider being tolerated. He belongs. He is a member of that church, with the same standing as the man who owns him. Paul does not argue for this or soften it or explain himself. He simply states it, in a public letter that would be read aloud in the room where Philemon was sitting.

Set that beside 3:11, a few paragraphs earlier: “here there is not Greek and Jew … slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.” Here is the doctrine walking through the door on two legs. Paul does not stage a revolt against Rome’s slave system; he does something slower and more corrosive to it. He puts a runaway and a delegate side by side, gives them the same name, and tells the church they are brothers. A system cannot survive many decades of that.

And there is a word here for anyone whose past would embarrass them in a church. Onesimus had a criminal record and everyone in the room knew it. The apostle’s public description of him is “faithful and beloved.” That is what the gospel does with a history: it does not pretend the history away, and it refuses to let it be the man’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men, and each carries a story worth pausing on.

“Aristarchus my fellow prisoner.” A Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4), he had been seized by the mob in the theatre at Ephesus (Acts 19:29) and had sailed with Paul on the voyage that ended in shipwreck (Acts 27:2). He is now in custody with him. The word Paul uses is literally fellow prisoner of war — a man captured alongside him in the same campaign. Some have thought he shared the imprisonment voluntarily, staying at Paul’s side when he need not have. Either way, here is a Christian whose name we would never have known but for a greeting, who followed the apostle into a riot, a shipwreck, and a cell.

“And Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions — if he comes to you, welcome him).” Read that carefully, because it is the sound of a wound healing. This is the John Mark who abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through the first missionary journey and went home (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas wanted to take him again, Paul refused, and the disagreement was sharp enough to split the two men and end their partnership (Acts 15:37–39).

And now Paul is writing ahead to make sure Mark gets a warm reception. He is even aware that a church might have heard the story and be wary — hence “welcome him.” Years later, at the very end, Paul will send for him: “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Tim. 4:11). The same word, useful, that Onesimus’s name means. The deserter became indispensable, and tradition holds he wrote the second Gospel. Grace does not discard those who have failed; it restores them, and it restores the people they failed, too.

“These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers.” Only three Jewish believers in Paul’s whole circle at that moment — and the word “only” carries a quiet ache in it. This is the man of Romans 9 who could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen. He is apostle to the Gentiles by calling, and it evidently cost him something to look around a room and count three of his own people. “They have been a comfort to me” is the only time Paul uses that particular word in all his letters; it is a medical term, the root behind “paregoric,” a soothing that eases pain.

One phrase here has puzzled readers: “fellow workers for the kingdom of God.” Paul speaks of the kingdom far less than Jesus does in the Gospels, and some conclude it is not the church’s present business — that it belongs to Israel, or waits wholly in the future. There is a real truth in that instinct and it should be honoured: the kingdom in its full visible glory is still to come, when Christ returns to reign.

But notice what Paul writes here — these men are, right now, fellow workers for it. And earlier in this very letter he said something more startling still: God “has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son” (1:13). Not will transfer. Has. So Scripture holds two truths and we must drop neither: the kingdom is already here, inaugurated wherever Christ is owned as King, and not yet consummated, awaiting his return in glory. We live in it now, and we labour for its advance, while we wait for its dawning in full (cf. Rom. 14:17; Acts 28:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras is the most important name in the list, because without him there would be no church at Colossae to write to. He was the man who first brought them the gospel — Paul called him “our beloved fellow servant, a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf” (1:7) — and it was his report that prompted this letter. He is far from home, with Paul, and Paul says he is on his knees.

“Always struggling on your behalf in his prayers.” The word is agonizomenos — the athlete’s straining word, the root of our “agony,” used of a wrestler in the contest. It is the same word Paul used of his own labour for them in 2:1. This is not a man who mentions Colossae in his devotions. He is wrestling.

That is worth letting land, because most of us think of intercession as the least strenuous thing a Christian does — the thing you offer when you cannot offer anything useful. Epaphras is hundreds of miles away and can do nothing else for these people, and the New Testament describes what he is doing as combat. If prayer is genuinely wrestling, then the person who says “all I can do is pray” has misunderstood which activity is the strenuous one.

Now mark the exact content of his prayer, because it is the whole letter distilled into one petition: “that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.” “Stand” — firm, not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). “Mature” is teleioi, full-grown, the goal Paul named in 1:28 — and note the sting, since the false teachers were offering an “advanced” inner circle. Paul’s maturity is not a grade above ordinary Christians; it is the growing-up of people already filled in Christ (2:10). “Fully assured” is a wonderful word meaning carried all the way to settled conviction — not tentative, not hedging. And all of it “in all the will of God”: not in esoteric secrets, but resting in the whole will of God made known in his Son.

Ask yourself what you actually pray for the people you love. Most of our praying, if we are honest, is for their circumstances to improve. Epaphras wrestles for their maturity and assurance. He wants them standing, grown, and certain. It is a larger ambition than comfort, and it is the one that survives whatever happens to their circumstances.

“He has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.” Three towns within about a dozen miles of one another in the Lycus valley — Colossae, Laodicea the wealthy banking centre, and Hierapolis with its hot springs. Epaphras had evidently evangelised the whole valley, and Paul, who had never been there, formally vouches for him: “I bear him witness.” It is a certificate written by a prisoner for a man whose work he had only heard about, and it is the sort of thing that steadies a congregation’s confidence in the person who taught them.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine words, two names, and between them one of the saddest contrasts in Scripture — though nobody reading the letter that day could have known it.

“Luke the beloved physician.” This is the author of the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, and it is the only place in the New Testament where we are told his trade. It explains a great deal about how he writes: the careful research, the orderly account “having followed all things closely” (Luke 1:3), the precise interest in illness that runs through his Gospel. He is also, in the “we” passages of Acts, a travelling companion who quietly writes himself into the story without ever naming himself.

“Beloved” is Paul’s own word for him, and the picture it opens is worth having. Paul was a man with a physical affliction he could not shake (2 Cor. 12:7; Gal. 4:13–14), flogged five times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times. Travelling with him, for years, was a doctor. Whatever else providence was doing in Paul’s life, it had arranged for a physician to be within reach — and at the very end, when everyone else has gone, Paul writes: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Tim. 4:11).

“As does Demas.” Three words, no title. Tychicus is a beloved brother, Onesimus is faithful and beloved, Epaphras is a servant of Christ Jesus, Luke is the beloved physician. Demas gets his name and nothing else — and whether or not Paul meant anything by the brevity, the sequel is on record. Years later: “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Tim. 4:10).

He is not accused of scandal or heresy. He fell in love with this present world — the ordinary, respectable pull of comfort, safety, and a quieter life — and the pull was stronger than his attachment to a chained old man in Rome. That is how most people leave. Not with a repudiation but with a drift.

So the verse holds the two possibilities of a Christian life side by side: the man who stayed to the end, and the man who did not. Both were in the room when this letter was sealed; both sent their greetings; nobody in Colossae could have told them apart. Not all who begin well finish well, and the New Testament never lets us forget it. Let it make us watchful rather than smug — and let it make us pray, as Epaphras did two verses earlier, that we may stand.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.”

Two things sit in this short verse, and both are easy to walk past. The first is Nympha herself. A woman is named, and a congregation meets in her home. For the first two centuries or more there were no church buildings anywhere; Christians met in houses, and the house had to be large enough and its owner willing to have it filled every week with people who might attract official attention. That means Nympha had means, and it means she used them. The New Testament names several such women — Lydia at Philippi (Acts 16:15), Priscilla with Aquila (1 Cor. 16:19), Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12) — and the early church would have been homeless without them.

The second is the shape of it. “The church in her house” tells you what a first-century congregation actually looked like: not a hall, but a room; not an audience, but a group small enough to eat together. When Paul writes about bearing with one another and forgiving each other (3:13), he is describing people who sat in the same room every week and could not avoid one another’s faults. Our arrangements are different. The demand is not.

And Laodicea keeps appearing — here, in verse 13, in verse 16. It lay about ten miles off, a rich banking town famous for its black wool and an eye-salve, and Paul is knitting these valley congregations together: greet them, swap letters with them, pray for them. They were not to be a self-contained little society.

There is a shadow over the name, though, for anyone who reads on. A generation later the risen Christ dictates a letter to this same church: “you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17). Paul greets them warmly here, and the warning is not yet needed. Churches can be greeted by an apostle and still drift. The Laodicea of Colossians 4 and the Laodicea of Revelation 3 are the same address.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.”

Start with the obvious thing that is not obvious to us: “read among you” means read aloud, to the gathered congregation. Almost nobody owned a book. Literacy was limited and copies were expensive, so for most Christians for most of the church’s history, Scripture came in through the ears in a room full of other people. Paul writes assuming his letter will be performed, not studied — which is worth remembering when a sentence in his letters runs long. He was writing for the ear.

Then the instruction itself, and it is more significant than it looks. From the very beginning these were public documents for the whole people of God, not private mail. Paul expects congregations to swap his letters, copy them, and read one another’s. That habit — churches passing letters around the Lycus valley and beyond — is the first stirring of what became the New Testament. Nobody convened to decide it; it began with an apostle telling one small church to share what it had.

And what was “the letter from Laodicea”? We do not know, and honesty serves better than invention here. It may simply be lost — a letter of Paul’s that God did not intend to preserve, which should not alarm us; the apostle wrote at least one other letter to Corinth we do not have (1 Cor. 5:9). Many have thought it is the circular we call Ephesians, going round the region and reaching Laodicea before Colossae. A forgery under that name appeared later and the church rightly refused it.

What the uncertainty does not touch is the doctrine of Scripture. That a letter written by an apostle might not be preserved is not a gap in the Bible; it means God gave his church what he meant it to have. The canon is not everything the apostles ever wrote. It is what God caused to be kept.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And say to Archippus, ‘See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.’”

We meet Archippus once more, in the letter to Philemon, where Paul calls him “our fellow soldier” and names him alongside Philemon and Apphia (Philem. 1–2) — probably a member of that household, quite possibly their son. Something had stalled. Paul does not say what, and there is no rebuke in the words, but the charge would not be needed if all were well.

Notice first that it is public. Paul does not write privately to Archippus; he tells the whole congregation to say it to him. There is a wisdom in that which cuts both ways. A church is meant to hold its members to what they have taken on — encouragement is a corporate duty, not merely a pastoral one — and a man who has gone quiet in his work is better served by a room full of people who expect something of him than by everyone politely looking away.

Then the two words that carry the charge. The ministry is one he has received — a trust handed to him, not a career he chose. That changes its character entirely: you may resign from a job you selected, but a trust is somebody else’s property left in your hands. And he is to fulfil it — literally to fill it full, to carry it through to the end. Not to begin it, not to maintain it respectably, but to finish.

There may be more here than we can see. Archippus belongs to Philemon’s household, and Philemon’s household is exactly where Onesimus is walking back to as this letter travels (v. 9). Whatever ministry had stalled, it had stalled in the one home in Colossae about to be tested hardest — the home that must decide how to receive a returning runaway. Paul does not join the two threads for us, and we should not force them. But he wrote both letters the same week and sent them by the same hand.

This is the only command in the entire roll-call, and it swings the whole list round to face the reader. Paul has just named a dozen people who carried letters, prayed, went to prison, came home, stayed, and left. Then, at the end, one imperative — and it lands on an ordinary Christian in a small town whose ministry we cannot even identify. You have been given something too. See that you finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.” Paul dictated his letters to a secretary — it was Tertius who actually penned Romans, and he says so (Rom. 16:22) — and at the close the apostle would take the pen himself. It served two purposes. It authenticated the letter, his handwriting the seal of genuineness against forgeries (2 Thess. 3:17); and it was a piece of pure affection, his own hand reaching across six hundred miles to a church that had never seen his face.

Then, in that handwriting, three words: “Remember my chains.”

Picture it exactly. A manacled hand takes the pen. Roman custody meant a wrist chained to a guard, and the iron would have moved and scraped as he wrote. This is the letter that has told us Christ is the image of the invisible God, that in him all things hold together, that in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. The man who wrote it was in irons while he wrote, and the last thing he does is ask them not to forget it.

It is not self-pity — there has not been a syllable of complaint in the whole letter. It is partly a request for prayer, which he asked for plainly in verse 3. But the chains are also an argument, and he knows it. Nobody wears irons for a lie. A church being offered a more sophisticated religion by teachers who risked nothing had been sent the gospel by a man paying for it in metal.

“Grace be with you.” The last word answers the first. The letter opened “grace to you and peace from God our Father” (1:2) and closes here, and everything between the two — the supremacy of Christ, the emptiness of the false teaching, the new life, the transformed household, the page of names — stands inside grace and is made of it.

To a congregation being told they could climb nearer to God by rules, festivals, visions, and severity to the body, the final word is the first word. Not effort. Not secret knowledge. Not a higher tier for the initiated. Grace — the free and inexhaustible gift of God in the Christ in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and in whom they have already been filled. From grace, to grace, all the way home.
